The Sauce Book

Nine sauces after BBQ — cooking recipes, production lines, machines, art. CONDIMENTAL, pre-alpha, 25 September 2026.

BBQ proved the shape: a second sauce does not need a second factory, it needs a tap — a pipe off a fluid the factory already makes, taken before the bottler. Everything below is built on that move. Seven of the nine sauces here are a data-file edit: recipes, ingredients, shop prices, contracts, and one voxel generator each. Two buy a whole new axis of play, and those two are where the interesting design risk lives.

How to read this

  • DATA — new entries in data/*.ron plus voxel generators. No Rust, no GDScript.
  • NEW MACHINE — the above, plus a machine kind and its model. Still no sim work.
  • NEW AXIS — the above, plus a rule the simulation does not have yet. Two sauces do this; both are called out with what exactly it costs.

Every kitchen recipe below is a real one, scaled and simplified until it maps onto a stage of the line. Every game recipe is written in the shape data/recipes.ron already uses, so it can be pasted in and argued with. Prices follow the shipped rule — a box's ingredients cost about a third of what a contract pays for it. Machine art is concept art: drawn in the game's real palette (assets/voxels/palette.ron), rendered with a sketch tool, not the shipped vengi pipeline. Item art for shipped things is the shipped icon.

1 · The sauce tree

Every arrow is a sauce used as an ingredient in another sauce. This is the argument for the whole document: a tree rather than a list means late capital pays off across every branch at once. Buying the emulsifier does not unlock mayonnaise, it unlocks mayonnaise and aioli and chilli mayo and tartare and burger sauce — five sellable sauces off one purchase. Three of the nine sauces below need no new machine and no new raw at all once their parents exist — 06, 07 and 09 are three recipe entries apiece (a blend, a bottle and a box) — and four of the remaining six need a raw and nothing more.

Four things on the diagram have no sauce above them — ketchup, mustard, hot sauce and the pickle branch each start at a raw you buy. Two of those are hubs, and they are deliberately different. Ketchup is the tutorial root, and by sauce 09 it is a supplier as much as a product: BBQ taps it, the house reserve takes it at one remove, and burger sauce taps it again. Mustard is the new root, and it is the busy one: it feeds honey mustard, it is an input to mayonnaise (mustard is the emulsifier in real mayonnaise, not a flavouring), and it lands in the house reserve. Put mustard early and everything downstream gets cheaper to reach.

One node on that tree is not a sauce. Pickles (the blue node) are feedstock — a thing the factory makes and never sells, the first of its kind in the game. Two sauces eat them and nobody ships them, which makes the pickle line the first bit of your factory that exists purely to serve another bit of your factory. That is a Factorio feeling the game does not have yet.

2 · The nine sauces

01 · Wholegrain Mustard — DATA

The point of it. The first sauce that is not ketchup-shaped, and the one that teaches fluid contention without a single new mechanic. It reuses every machine kind in the game and still forces a rebuild, because it drinks four vinegar a batch where ketchup drinks two. One tank cannot feed both lines. The splitter you have never needed becomes the answer.

In a kitchen

100 g yellow mustard seed and 40 g brown, soaked 24 hours in 150 ml cider vinegar and 50 ml water. Add 1 tsp ground turmeric, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp honey. Pulse-grind half the seed and leave the rest whole — that split is what makes it wholegrain. Warm gently to 60 °C for twenty minutes to knock back the raw bite, then rest two days before jarring; mustard is unpleasantly harsh on day one and rounds out on day three. (The rest is the one thing the game will not model — see §8.)

In the game

Recipe(id: "mustard_grits", inputs: [("mustard_seed", 3)],
       outputs: [("mustard_grits", 1)], machine: "crusher", time_ticks: 70),
Recipe(id: "mustard_mix", inputs: [("mustard_grits", 1), ("turmeric", 1)],
       fluid_inputs: [("vinegar", 4)], fluid_outputs: [("mustard_mix", 1)],
       machine: "mixer", time_ticks: 90),
Recipe(id: "mustard", fluid_inputs: [("mustard_mix", 1)],
       fluid_outputs: [("mustard", 1)], machine: "cooking_vat", time_ticks: 180),
Recipe(id: "bottled_mustard", fluid_inputs: [("mustard", 1)],
       outputs: [("bottled_mustard", 1)], machine: "bottler", time_ticks: 60),
Recipe(id: "boxed_mustard", inputs: [("bottled_mustard", 1)],
       outputs: [("boxed_mustard", 1)], machine: "packer", time_ticks: 40),

The line

Hopper of mustard seed → crusher (70t, mills the seed to grits) → belt → mixer (90t, grits plus a hopper of turmeric, drinking vinegar from a tank) → pipe → cooking vat (180t, a warm steep, not a reduction — shorter than ketchup's 240) → pipe → bottler → belt → packer → dock. Structurally it is the ketchup chain with different ids, which is the point: a player who can build ketchup can build this on muscle memory, and then discovers the vinegar bill.

Machines

None new. A second crusher recipe, and a third on the mixer, the cooking vat, the bottler and the packer — every kind already on your floor. This is where the recipe-ambiguity problem bites (§7): ketchup_mix and mustard_mix both run on the mixer and both consume vinegar, which the shipped invariant test forbids. That decision has to be made before this sauce can ship.

Why it is fun

Because the trap is legible and the fix is satisfying. You build the mustard line, both lines run for ninety seconds, and then both starve — not one. The vinegar tank is the shared thing and nothing on screen said so. The fix is a second tank, or a splitter with a real decision about which side gets priority. It is the first time the factory pushes back on a resource rather than on geometry, and it costs no new code to teach.

The money

18 per box in ingredients (seed 2×3, turmeric 4, vinegar 2×4). Ketchup is 11, BBQ is 23. Contracts pay 48–56 — deliberately thin, because the sauce's job is to make you fix your plumbing, not to make you rich. Gate: 25 lifetime deliveries, releasing mustard_seed, turmeric and the mustard contracts.

02 · Honey Mustard — DATA

The point of it. Three lines in recipes.ron and one new raw — and the first sauce in the game that is never cooked. It taps the mustard run before the bottler and goes straight to a mixer and out. A derived sauce that skips the slowest machine is free throughput, and that is a lesson worth teaching exactly once.

In a kitchen

Three parts finished wholegrain mustard, two parts honey, one part cider vinegar, a pinch of salt. Whisk cold. Do not heat it: honey's aromatics are volatile and heat drives them off, leaving sugar — which is why this is a blend and not a cook, in the kitchen and in the game.

In the game

Recipe(id: "honey_mustard", fluid_inputs: [("mustard", 1), ("honey", 1)],
       fluid_outputs: [("honey_mustard", 1)], machine: "mixer", time_ticks: 110),
Recipe(id: "bottled_honey_mustard", fluid_inputs: [("honey_mustard", 1)],
       outputs: [("bottled_honey_mustard", 1)], machine: "bottler", time_ticks: 60),
Recipe(id: "boxed_honey_mustard", inputs: [("bottled_honey_mustard", 1)],
       outputs: [("boxed_honey_mustard", 1)], machine: "packer", time_ticks: 40),

The line

A pipe off the mustard vat's run — the same tap BBQ takes off ketchup — into a mixer (110t, cold blend) fed by a tank of honey. Pipe to a bottler, belt to a packer, belt to the dock. Three machines and a dock. It is the shortest sellable line in the game — only chilli mayo (06) ever matches it — and it should stay that way.

Machines

None new. One more mixer recipe, one more bottler recipe, one more packer recipe.

Why it is fun

It is the reward beat. Mustard just cost you a rebuild; honey mustard is three machines bolted to the side of it that sells for more per box than mustard does. It also quietly teaches the tap as a tactic rather than a curiosity: you now have two sauces competing for one mustard run, and the question "do I bottle it or blend it?" has a board-driven answer that changes every few minutes.

The money

22 per box, of which 18 is mustard you made yourself — the first sauce whose bill is mostly your own labour. Contracts pay 58–64. Gate: 35 lifetime deliveries, releasing honey and the honey-mustard contracts.

03 · Mayonnaise — NEW MACHINE + NEW AXIS

The point of it. The cold-chain tier. Two new machines, and the first ingredient in the game that can go off. Mayonnaise is where the factory stops being a graph of throughputs and starts being a floor plan with a clock on it.

In a kitchen

Two egg yolks, 1 tsp mustard, 1 tbsp vinegar or lemon juice, a pinch of salt. Whisk, then add 250 ml neutral oil a drop at a time at first, in a thin stream once it takes. Everything at room temperature or the emulsion splits; the finished jar goes straight to the fridge. The mustard is not flavouring — it is the emulsifier, which is why mustard is an input in the game recipe and why mustard has to exist before mayonnaise can.

In the game

Recipe(id: "mayo_base", inputs: [("egg", 2)],
       fluid_inputs: [("oil", 3), ("mustard", 1)],
       fluid_outputs: [("mayo_base", 1)],
       machine: "emulsifier", time_ticks: 150),
Recipe(id: "mayonnaise", fluid_inputs: [("mayo_base", 1)],
       fluid_outputs: [("mayonnaise", 1)],
       machine: "chiller", time_ticks: 90),
Recipe(id: "bottled_mayonnaise", fluid_inputs: [("mayonnaise", 1)],
       outputs: [("bottled_mayonnaise", 1)], machine: "bottler", time_ticks: 60),
Recipe(id: "boxed_mayonnaise", inputs: [("bottled_mayonnaise", 1)],
       outputs: [("boxed_mayonnaise", 1)], machine: "packer", time_ticks: 40),

The line

A hopper of eggs, a tank of oil and a tap off the mustard run all meet at the emulsifier (150t — slow, and visibly slow: the dosing arm is the animation). Pipe to the chiller (90t), pipe to the bottler, belt, packer, dock. Two fluid draws at one machine is a move BBQ's cook already ships — but taking them alongside a solid is not, so mayo_base is the first recipe in the game to do both at once. That is a combination of two exercised paths rather than a new capability, and it is where the shape gets its first test; sauces 08 and 09 inherit it. What is new for the player is that the feed belt from the egg hopper is now a liability.

Machines

Emulsifier (new, 1×2, manufacturing 1, 180) and Chiller (new, 1×2, manufacturing 1, 150). Full specs in §3. The chiller is the only white machine on the floor, so cold reads at a glance across the whole factory.

Why it is fun

Because for the first time the thing beating you is your own floor plan. Eggs spoil: a spoil clock runs on every buffer that is not a chiller, and a long, pretty, sprawling feed belt now kills stock outright before it arrives. Compact wins; sprawl rots. It inverts the habit the first four hours taught — long belts are cheap, so make them long — and it does it with one number on one ingredient. The chiller then becomes a verb: players will start parking chillers as buffers, which is exactly the emergent use worth designing for.

The money

33 per box (egg 3×2, oil 3×3, plus 18 of mustard). Contracts pay 92–104 — the first real jump in the game, and it should feel like one. Gate: 45 lifetime deliveries, releasing egg, oil and the mayonnaise contracts. The emulsifier and the chiller are simply on sale from a new game: data/unlocks.ron has no field that holds a machine back, and §6 says what adding one would cost.

04 · Garlic Aioli — DATA

The point of it. A variant, not a tier: one crusher recipe and one more emulsifier recipe on machines you already own. Aioli steals mayonnaise exactly the way BBQ steals ketchup — same run, same contention — and what it adds is a contract board that can ask for both.

In a kitchen

Four garlic cloves and half a teaspoon of coarse salt pounded to a smooth paste in a mortar — the salt is the abrasive, so do not skip it — then folded into 250 ml of mayonnaise with lemon to taste. Traditional Catalan allioli is garlic and oil alone, emulsified by hand, and is a nightmare; every restaurant kitchen on earth cheats with mayonnaise, so the game cheats too.

In the game

Recipe(id: "garlic_paste", inputs: [("garlic", 2), ("salt", 1)],
       outputs: [("garlic_paste", 1)], machine: "crusher", time_ticks: 80),
Recipe(id: "aioli", inputs: [("garlic_paste", 1)],
       fluid_inputs: [("mayonnaise", 1)], fluid_outputs: [("aioli", 1)],
       machine: "emulsifier", time_ticks: 90),
Recipe(id: "bottled_aioli", fluid_inputs: [("aioli", 1)],
       outputs: [("bottled_aioli", 1)], machine: "bottler", time_ticks: 60),
Recipe(id: "boxed_aioli", inputs: [("bottled_aioli", 1)],
       outputs: [("boxed_aioli", 1)], machine: "packer", time_ticks: 40),

The line

Hoppers of garlic and salt → crusher (80t) → belt → a second emulsifier (90t) tapping the mayonnaise run → bottler → packer → dock. Note the second emulsifier: the first one is saturated making mayo base at 150t, so aioli is also the moment a player learns to buy a duplicate of a machine rather than a new kind.

Machines

None new. A third crusher recipe and a second emulsifier recipe. Under §7's recommended rule these are unambiguous — mayo_base needs eggs and aioli needs garlic paste, so what the machine is plumbed to still decides what it runs.

Why it is fun

Because it makes the board harder without making the factory harder. "40 mayonnaise and 20 aioli" is a genuinely nastier order than "60 of either" off one mayo run, and the player has to decide whether to split the run, stagger the contracts, or buy a third emulsifier. That is a scheduling problem, and the game has not posed one yet.

The money

38 per box, 33 of it mayonnaise. Contracts pay 104–118. Gate: 60 lifetime deliveries, releasing garlic, salt and the aioli contracts.

05 · Hot Sauce — NEW MACHINE + NEW AXIS

The point of it. The acid tier. A 3 000-tick ferment and — for the first time — a factory that has to grow sideways.

There is one hot sauce in this game and it is fermented. Hot sauce is a category in the real world with two production routes — quick, where vinegar supplies the acid, and fermented, where lactic acid bacteria make it over weeks — and the game only wants one of them. The ferment is the route worth simulating, because a process that takes 3 000 ticks is a design problem and a process that takes 120 is a formality. So the sauce is called Hot Sauce, its fluid id is hot_sauce, and the fermenter in the middle of its line is simply how it is made. Every later reference — chilli mayo's second tap, house reserve's third draw — is this one fluid.

A second, unfermented "quick hot sauce" is a real option and is deliberately not taken: a cheap alternative standing next to the fermenter would undercut the one thing the fermenter exists to be, which is slow. It belongs on the §5 list later, if ever, once players have built a fermenter bank and have opinions about it.

In a kitchen

500 g red chillies, stems off, blended coarse with 15 g salt — 3 % by weight, which is the whole recipe's only real number. Pack into a jar under an airlock, leave at 20 °C for one to three weeks until it stops bubbling and smells sour rather than sweet. Blend with 100 ml vinegar, strain, and pasteurise to 80 °C so it stops changing in the bottle. The ferment is what separates a hot sauce from hot vinegar, and it is slow: this is genuinely the longest process in this document.

In the game

Recipe(id: "chilli_mash", inputs: [("chilli", 3), ("salt", 1)],
       outputs: [("chilli_mash", 1)], machine: "crusher", time_ticks: 80),
Recipe(id: "fermented_mash", inputs: [("chilli_mash", 1)],
       fluid_outputs: [("fermented_mash", 1)],
       machine: "fermenter", time_ticks: 3000),
Recipe(id: "hot_sauce", fluid_inputs: [("fermented_mash", 1), ("vinegar", 2)],
       fluid_outputs: [("hot_sauce", 1)],
       machine: "cooking_vat", time_ticks: 120),
Recipe(id: "bottled_hot_sauce", fluid_inputs: [("hot_sauce", 1)],
       outputs: [("bottled_hot_sauce", 1)], machine: "bottler", time_ticks: 60),
Recipe(id: "boxed_hot_sauce", inputs: [("bottled_hot_sauce", 1)],
       outputs: [("boxed_hot_sauce", 1)], machine: "packer", time_ticks: 40),

The line

Hoppers of chilli and salt → crusher (80t) → belt → fermenter (3 000t, 2×2) → lined pipe → cooking vat (120t, pasteurise, drinking vinegar) → pipe → bottler → packer → dock. Only the first run is corrosive. The raw mash is the live, acid-making thing and pasteurising in the vat is exactly what stops it — so finished hot sauce travels in ordinary pipe, and so does every later tap off it (06, 07). That matters: if the finished fluid were corrosive too, chilli mayo would stop being free.

Machines

Fermenter (new, 2×2, manufacturing 2, 260) and lined pipe (new, 1×1, no crew, 24 — three times plain pipe). Full specs in §3.

Why it is fun

One fermenter makes a unit every hundred seconds. Nothing you build downstream fixes that — a faster vat, a second bottler, more staff, none of it matters. The only answer is a bank of fermenters, so for the first time the factory grows sideways instead of longer, and a corner of the floor becomes a farm of slow identical machines quietly bubbling. That is a Factorio feeling the game does not have yet, and it is worth a machine kind to get.

The corrosion rule is the second half: it means you cannot simply reuse the pipe you have lying around. A player who runs plain pipe on fermented mash will watch it fault mid-shift, and the fix is obvious, cheap and memorable — which is what a good punishment looks like.

The money

11 per box (chilli 2×3, salt 1, vinegar 2×2) — the cheapest bill in the game — and contracts pay 66–74. It is deliberately the best margin per box and the worst margin per minute: you can only make so much of it, so you are buying patience, not profit. Gate: 75 lifetime deliveries, releasing chilli and the hot-sauce contracts. As with mayonnaise, the fermenter and the lined pipe are on sale from the start — what gates the tier is the chilli, not the kit.

06 · Chilli Mayo — DATA

The point of it. The cross-product. Two tiers you have already paid for, meeting at one mixer for the price of a data edit. Nothing is bought and nothing is built.

In a kitchen

Four parts mayonnaise to one part hot sauce, folded in with a spatula rather than whisked — whisking shears the emulsion and you get a thin pink liquid instead of a sauce. A squeeze of lime and a pinch of smoked paprika if you want the chipotle version.

In the game

Recipe(id: "chilli_mayo", fluid_inputs: [("mayonnaise", 2), ("hot_sauce", 1)],
       fluid_outputs: [("chilli_mayo", 1)],
       machine: "mixer", time_ticks: 80),
Recipe(id: "bottled_chilli_mayo", fluid_inputs: [("chilli_mayo", 1)],
       outputs: [("bottled_chilli_mayo", 1)], machine: "bottler", time_ticks: 60),
Recipe(id: "boxed_chilli_mayo", inputs: [("bottled_chilli_mayo", 1)],
       outputs: [("boxed_chilli_mayo", 1)], machine: "packer", time_ticks: 40),

The line

Two taps — one off the mayonnaise run, one off the hot sauce run — into a mixer (80t), then bottler, packer, dock. Three machines and a dock, all of kinds you own, and the two taps are the entire build.

Machines

None. Not one.

Why it is fun

Because unlocking hot sauce quietly unlocked this too, and the player finds out by reading the contract board. It is the whole argument for a sauce tree rather than a sauce list: late capital pays off across every branch at once, and the most expensive thing in the book (the fermenter bank) suddenly has a second customer. It also raises the stakes on the mayo run for a third time — mayonnaise, aioli and chilli mayo all drink from it — which is the point at which a player stops extending the factory and starts re-planning it.

The money

77 per box, all of it sauce you made. Contracts pay 210–235 — the biggest line in the book until tartare turns up at 08. Gate: 95 lifetime deliveries, which is comfortably past both parents; there is no gate on the recipe itself, because in practice the tree is the gate — without a mayonnaise run and a hot sauce run there is nothing to tap.

07 · House Reserve Steak Sauce — DATA

The point of it. Tier 7, and not one new machine. It is gated by your floor plan: three pipe runs and a hopper into one 2×2 vat, without crossing.

In a kitchen

Equal parts tomato-based BBQ sauce and wholegrain mustard, a quarter part hot sauce, two tablespoons of molasses, a splash of vinegar. Reduce twenty minutes until it coats a spoon (nappe — it should hold a line drawn through it on the back of the spoon). Bottle hot and wax the cap. It is a steakhouse table sauce: sweet, sour, sharp and hot at once, which is exactly what makes it the top of the tree — it needs one sauce from every branch.

In the game

Recipe(id: "house_reserve", inputs: [("molasses", 1)],
       fluid_inputs: [("bbq", 1), ("mustard", 1), ("hot_sauce", 1)],
       fluid_outputs: [("house_reserve", 1)],
       machine: "cooking_vat", time_ticks: 400),
Recipe(id: "bottled_house_reserve", fluid_inputs: [("house_reserve", 1)],
       outputs: [("bottled_house_reserve", 1)], machine: "bottler", time_ticks: 60),
Recipe(id: "boxed_house_reserve", inputs: [("bottled_house_reserve", 1)],
       outputs: [("boxed_house_reserve", 1)], machine: "packer", time_ticks: 40),

The line

Three taps — BBQ, mustard, hot sauce — plus a hopper of molasses, all into one cooking vat (400t). Pipe out to a bottler (the wax dip is cosmetic), belt, packer, dock.

Three fluid draws at one machine has never shipped. BBQ's cook draws two, and the fluid scope was widened to two for it; the registry holds a list and does not cap it, but the code path has never been exercised at three, so this needs a test before it needs anything else.

Machines

None new. A fifth cooking-vat recipe, a ninth bottler recipe, a ninth packer recipe.

Why it is fun

A 2×2 vat has eight perimeter tiles and the outlet face eats two of them. Three pipe runs and a hopper have to reach the remaining six without crossing each other or the three lines already running through that part of your factory. That is the whole puzzle, and it is a spatial one — the payoff tier of the game is a layout tier, and it costs nothing to build but a rethink. Players will tear down a quarter of the floor to make room for it, and that teardown is the memorable bit.

The money

56 per box — three sauces you chose not to ship, plus molasses. Contracts pay 190–210. Note that it pays less per box than chilli mayo while eating three finished sauces instead of two: the house reserve is a prestige sauce, and what it really costs you is three finished runs diverted away from orders you could have filled. Gate: 150 lifetime deliveries — past every branch it draws from. It releases no ingredient at all: the only thing this tier unlocks is contracts, because everything it consumes you already make.

P · Pickles — DATA, AND NOT A SAUCE

The point of it. The last two sauces in this book are both pickle sauces, so the pickle line is drawn once, here, and both of them tap it. It is the first thing the factory makes that nobody buys: there is no bottled pickle, no boxed pickle and no pickle contract. It exists to feed two mixers, and that is the entire point of it.

In a kitchen

Small ridged cucumbers, scrubbed, packed upright in a jar with 3 % brine, a splash of vinegar and a head of dill. Left at room temperature they go cloudy in two days and sour in a week — that cloud is the lactic ferment, the same one the hot sauce mash runs, but a quick pickle is days where a chilli mash is weeks. Drain, top and tail, and dice to 3 mm: tartare wants it fine enough to spread, not to crunch.

In the game

Recipe(id: "pickles", inputs: [("cucumber", 3), ("salt", 1)],
       fluid_inputs: [("vinegar", 1)],
       outputs: [("pickle", 1)],
       machine: "fermenter", time_ticks: 600),
Recipe(id: "diced_pickle", inputs: [("pickle", 1)],
       outputs: [("diced_pickle", 1)], machine: "crusher", time_ticks: 80),

The line

Hoppers of cucumber and salt, and a pipe of vinegar, into a fermenter (600t — twenty seconds, a fifth of the hot sauce mash, because a quick brine pickle is not a months-long ferment and should not cost like one) → belt → crusher (80t, dicing rather than pulping) → belt. That belt is the output. It goes to a mixer, or to two mixers, and never to a bottler.

Machines

None new, and this is the nice part: the fermenter earns a second recipe and the crusher a fifth. If hot sauce has already been built, the bank of fermenters standing on the floor is suddenly dual-use, and the player's most expensive purchase in the book gets a second job without buying anything. Note that pickles and fermented_mash share no input id at all, so the fermenter needs nothing from §7 — it is disjoint under the shipped rule.

Why it is fun

A sub-assembly. Every factory game's moment of no return is the first line you build that has no customer outside the factory, and CONDIMENTAL does not have one yet — every belt today ends at a dock. The pickle line ends at a junction. It also makes a ratio problem out of nothing, and the numbers are pleasingly awkward: a fermenter yields one pickle per 600 ticks, a crusher dices one per 80, and a tartare mixer eats one per 100. So six fermenters and one crusher feed one mixer — the crusher has headroom to spare and the fermenter bank does not, which is the same lesson hot sauce teaches, arriving a second time in a form the player can now do arithmetic about.

The money

9 per unit of diced pickle in ingredients (cucumber 2×3, salt 1, vinegar 2×1), and one crate of cucumbers makes one pail. No contract, ever. The cost lands in the two sauces below.

08 · Tartare — DATA

The point of it. Mayonnaise with things in it. Every sauce shipped or proposed so far is a flat colour; tartare is the first one with visible bits, which makes it the first bottle on the shelf you can identify at play zoom without reading a label.

In a kitchen

Two parts mayonnaise, one part finely diced gherkin, a heaped spoon of capers chopped just enough to bleed, a squeeze of lemon, parsley, and black pepper. Do not rinse the capers — the brine is the seasoning. Rest it thirty minutes: it is watery at first and thickens as the pickle gives up its liquid into the emulsion.

In the game

Recipe(id: "tartare", inputs: [("diced_pickle", 1), ("capers", 1)],
       fluid_inputs: [("mayonnaise", 2)],
       fluid_outputs: [("tartare", 1)],
       machine: "mixer", time_ticks: 100),
Recipe(id: "bottled_tartare", fluid_inputs: [("tartare", 1)],
       outputs: [("bottled_tartare", 1)], machine: "bottler", time_ticks: 60),
Recipe(id: "boxed_tartare", inputs: [("bottled_tartare", 1)],
       outputs: [("boxed_tartare", 1)], machine: "packer", time_ticks: 40),

The line

A tap off the mayonnaise run, a belt of diced pickle from the crusher and a hopper of capers, all into a mixer (100t), then bottler, packer, dock. Mechanically this is bbq_mix's shipped shape exactly: two solids and one fluid at a mixer. What is new is where a solid comes from — diced pickle arrives off a line, not out of a hopper the player tops up.

Machines

None new. A sixth mixer recipe, a tenth bottler recipe, a tenth packer recipe.

Why it is fun

It is the first sauce whose art is a mechanic you can see. The flecks in the bottle are the pickle you routed, and a player who has just spent five minutes on a sub-assembly gets a bottle that visibly contains it. It is also the first sauce that can starve because a line you built is too slow rather than because a hopper ran dry — every solid input in the game today comes from a raw you buy, so "my crusher cannot keep up" is a sentence CONDIMENTAL has never made a player say. Beyond that it puts a fourth straw in the mayonnaise run, which is the pressure the mayo tier exists to create.

The money

81 per box: 66 of mayonnaise, 9 of diced pickle, 6 of capers. Contracts pay 225–250. Capers at 6 are the priciest raw in the book and they are only ever bought one at a time, which is deliberate — it is a small, steady drip of money leaving the factory rather than a bulk order, and it is the first ingredient a player will think about skipping. Gate: 170 lifetime deliveries, releasing cucumber, capers and the tartare contracts.

09 · Burger Sauce — DATA

The point of it. The sauce that eats the tutorial. Burger sauce is mayonnaise, ketchup and pickle — and ketchup is the thing the player has been making since the first minute of the game. This is the tier where the starter line stops being the boring one.

In a kitchen

Four parts mayonnaise, two parts ketchup, one part finely diced gherkin, a teaspoon of the pickle brine, a pinch of paprika and a pinch of onion powder. That is genuinely the whole recipe — every burger sauce on every menu is a variation on those three things, and the ratio is what is being argued about, not the ingredients.

In the game

Recipe(id: "burger_sauce", inputs: [("diced_pickle", 1)],
       fluid_inputs: [("mayonnaise", 2), ("ketchup", 1)],
       fluid_outputs: [("burger_sauce", 1)],
       machine: "mixer", time_ticks: 100),
Recipe(id: "bottled_burger_sauce", fluid_inputs: [("burger_sauce", 1)],
       outputs: [("bottled_burger_sauce", 1)], machine: "bottler", time_ticks: 60),
Recipe(id: "boxed_burger_sauce", inputs: [("bottled_burger_sauce", 1)],
       outputs: [("boxed_burger_sauce", 1)], machine: "packer", time_ticks: 40),

The line

Two taps — mayonnaise and ketchup — plus a belt of diced pickle, into a mixer (100t), then bottler, packer, dock. Both halves of that are shipped: BBQ's cook already draws two fluids, and BBQ's mixer already takes a solid alongside a fluid. Two fluids and a solid at one machine first appears earlier in this book, at 03, in mayo_base — so by the time burger sauce lands the shape is exercised and, unlike house reserve's three draws (07), it needs nothing new at all.

Machines

None new. A seventh mixer recipe, an eleventh bottler recipe, an eleventh packer recipe.

Why it is fun

Because it reaches all the way back to tile one. Ketchup has been a finished product for the whole game; here it becomes an ingredient, and the player has to tap the oldest, most settled pipe on their floor — the one they laid before they knew what they were doing — and steal from it. Some players will find their original ketchup line cannot spare the throughput and will have to go back and widen the thing they built first. That is the best kind of late-game content: it makes you re-read your own early work.

It is also the sauce that makes the tree look like a tree. Burger sauce and the house reserve are the only two nodes with three parents, and burger sauce is the one whose parents reach back to tile one — on the diagram the ketchup arrow runs the full width of the page to get to it.

The money

86 per box: 66 of mayonnaise, 11 of ketchup, 9 of diced pickle. Contracts pay 235–260, the best line in the book — and it should be, because it is the only sauce that competes with your own ketchup orders for supply. Every box of burger sauce is a box of ketchup you did not ship. Gate: 195 lifetime deliveries, releasing the burger-sauce contracts and nothing else: it introduces no raw of its own, and the cucumbers its pickles are made from arrived with tartare.

3 · Four things to build

Two sauces out of nine need new equipment — and the other seven need none at all, which is the tree paying for itself. This is all of it — three entries in data/machines.ron, four in data/shop.ron (a pipe is priced there without being a machine kind, exactly as plain pipe is today), and four voxel generators. The models above are concept art in the game's palette; they are not shipped assets.

Emulsifier — 1×2, manufacturing 1, 180

Threads oil into yolk under a high-shear head. Sits between the mixer (100) and the cooking vat (200) in price, and takes the same crew as a mixer. Visually the dosing line is the tell: a brass line running down from a small tank into the vessel, dripping. It is the only machine in the game where you can see the slow step, which matters because 150 ticks with no visible reason feels broken and 150 ticks with a dripping line feels deliberate. Cost to build: one data entry and one generator. No simulation work at all.

Chiller — 1×2, manufacturing 1, 150

Sets mayonnaise cold, and — the important part — while stock sits in a chiller's buffer, the spoil clock stops. It is the only white machine on the floor, with a frost window on the seen face, so "this part of my factory is cold" reads from the camera without a single UI element. Cost to build: one data entry, one generator, and the perishable axis (§6).

Fermenter — 2×2, manufacturing 2, 260

3 000 ticks, five times the longest process currently in the game (BBQ's cook, at 600). A 2×2 footprint and a two-person crew, so a bank of four is a real investment in floor and in payroll. Airlock bubbles on the lid are the motion frames — a machine that takes a hundred seconds needs to visibly be doing something the whole time — and a hazard band around the base says acid-rated, which is the visual link to lined pipe. It is the one new machine whose two recipes come from unrelated tiers — chilli mash for 05, cucumbers for the pickle line — so a bank bought for hot sauce is already paid for when tartare arrives. Cost to build: one data entry and one generator. No simulation work.

Lined pipe — 1×1, no crew, 24

Three times the price of plain pipe (8) and identical in every way except that a corrosive fluid does not eat it. Visually: the same pipe silhouette with an acid-yellow stripe, so a corrosive run is legible as a run rather than as a tooltip. Cost to build: one data entry, one generator, and the corrosion axis (§6).

4 · Ten new raws

Everything the nine sauces buy that the factory cannot make for itself. Prices sit where the shipped ones do (tomato 1, sugar 3, vinegar 2, liquid smoke 3, molasses 4, spice mix 5): a box of sauce costs about a third of what a contract pays for it.

Eight of the ten are hopper solids, which is deliberate: tanks are expensive in floor space, and a tier whose new raw is a fluid should be a tier that earns it.

Once the tree exists, a new sellable sauce is one interesting recipe entry and a colour — plus the bottler and packer pair every sauce in this book needs, which the table does not count because it is never the decision. These six are not proposals so much as evidence — they are what the tree is for, and they are the pool to draw from when a milestone needs content and has no budget.

6 · What this actually costs in code

Honest accounting. Seven of the nine sauces are data and art: recipes, ingredients, shop entries, contracts, unlocks, and one voxel generator per new thing. Two rules do not exist yet, and each is the price of admission for exactly one tier — and so for everything the tree hangs off it — which makes each a genuine go/no-go decision rather than a detail.

The perishable axis — buys mayonnaise (and everything downstream of it)

The rule. An ingredient may carry a shelf life in ticks. A stack of it sitting in a buffer — a hopper, a belt, a machine's input slot — ages; when its clock runs out it is destroyed and the loss is announced. A chiller's buffer does not run the clock.

What it touches. One optional field in data/ingredients.ron (shelf_life_ticks, absent meaning imperishable, so every existing entry is unchanged). A per-stack age in whatever holds a stack, which is the part to be careful about: ages must be fixed-point or integer ticks, they must be saved, and the save format changes. An event so the HUD can say what rotted and where, because silent destruction is indistinguishable from a bug.

What it is worth. It is the only rule in this document that changes how the whole factory is laid out rather than what it contains. Everything else here adds nodes to a graph; this one adds a cost to distance. That is a big lever for one field and one clock, and it is why mayonnaise is the tier worth arguing about.

The cheap version, if the answer is no. Make eggs imperishable and let mayonnaise be a straightforward two-new-machine tier. It loses the floor-plan lesson entirely and the chiller becomes decorative, but the sauce, the art and the economy all still work. Do not ship the chiller without the clock — a machine whose only job is to stop a clock that does not exist is a lie on the floor.

The corrosion axis — buys hot sauce

The rule. A fluid may be corrosive. A plain pipe carrying a corrosive fluid accumulates wear and eventually faults; lined pipe never does. Wear is visible on the pipe before it faults — this must not be a surprise.

What it touches. One optional field on a fluid, a per-pipe wear counter (saved), a fault state pipes do not currently have, and a tint or overlay on a worn pipe. It reuses whatever the andon stack-light work already gives machines for saying "something is wrong here".

What it is worth. Less than the perishable axis, honestly. Its real job is making the fermenter bank feel like specialist equipment rather than just another machine — you are building an acid corner of the factory, and it looks like one. That is a mood, not a mechanic.

The cheap version, if the answer is no. Drop corrosion, keep lined pipe as a pure requirement: a corrosive fluid simply cannot enter a plain pipe, refused at placement time the way an invalid connection already is. No wear, no clock, no save change — and it still forces the player to buy and route special pipe. This is the recommended fallback and it is close to free.

One thing the gates cannot say

Every Gate line in this document is written as a lifetime-delivery count, because that is the only trigger data/unlocks.ron has, and an Unlock names exactly two lists: ingredients and contracts. There is no field that holds a machine back. So the emulsifier, the chiller and the fermenter are all on sale from a new game, and what actually gates those tiers is that their raws cannot be bought and nobody is asking for the sauce — the same mechanism BBQ already ships with.

That is fine, and probably correct: a machine you can buy and cannot use is a worse lesson than a machine that appears when there is something to do with it. But if the shop list should grow as the game does, that is a third list on Unlock, a filter in the shop, and a Buy command that refuses a locked kind — small, but sim work, and it is not costed anywhere above.

7 · Decide this first

There is one shipped invariant that every sauce in this document runs into, and it has to be settled before any of them can land. From sim_core/src/sim/recipe.rs:

Recipes sharing a machine kind must take disjoint inputs, so that
what a machine is plumbed to *is* which recipe it runs and file
order never decides anything.

It is a good rule and it is load-bearing: it is the reason a machine needs no recipe dropdown. The proposals above break it in four places:

  • mixer: ketchup_mix and mustard_mix both consume vinegar.
  • crusher: garlic_paste and chilli_mash both consume salt.
  • mixer, again: chilli_mayo, tartare and burger_sauce all consume mayonnaise, and the last two also share diced_pickle.
  • mixer, a third time: bbq_mix and burger_sauce both consume ketchup — one shipped recipe and one proposed one, which is the clearest evidence that this is structural and not a slip in the proposals.

The first two are shared commodities — the kind of ingredient that ought to be shared. The last two are worse and more interesting: by sauce 09 the mixer hosts seven recipes drawn from an overlapping pool of inputs, most of them things the factory makes itself, which is what a sauce tree inevitably produces. This will happen again with sugar and with oil. There are three ways out.

A — Dodge it in data

Give each sauce its own raw: cider_vinegar for mustard, salt folded into the fermenter recipe instead of the crusher. Costs no code at all. Costs the player a second vinegar tank for no reason they can see, and multiplies ingredient ids forever — by sauce twelve there are four vinegars. Not recommended, but it is the escape hatch if the release is close.

B — Relax the invariant (recommended)

Replace "disjoint inputs" with: of any two recipes on one machine kind, each must require at least one input id the other does not — neither's input set may be a subset of the other's. A machine then runs the one recipe all of whose inputs it is actually plumbed to. All three violations above resolve cleanly: a mixer fed tomato paste, sugar and vinegar can only be making ketchup mix; a crusher fed garlic and salt can only be making garlic paste; a mixer fed mayonnaise, ketchup and diced pickle can only be making burger sauce.

Ambiguity is not impossible under this rule, and pretending otherwise is the trap. The subset rule stops one recipe from swallowing another, but it does nothing about a machine plumbed to the union of two — and the union satisfies both. Tartare needs mayonnaise, diced pickle and capers; burger sauce needs mayonnaise, ketchup and diced pickle; neither is a subset of the other, and a mixer reached by all four of those inputs qualifies for both. That is not a hypothetical, it is sauces 08 and 09 sitting next to each other.

So the rule needs a stated answer for it, and "whichever is first in the file" is exactly the answer the shipped invariant exists to forbid. The answer should be: a machine that qualifies for two recipes runs neither. It stops, it lights its andon amber, and its panel says which two it is torn between and asks the player to pick — the recipe dropdown of option C, but appearing only in the one case where the factory genuinely has not said what it wants, and disappearing again when a pipe is moved. Placement stays the language; the dropdown becomes the error message.

The property the original test protects — file order never decides anything — survives intact, which is the part that actually matters.

What it costs: rewrite the invariant test to the new rule, change recipe selection to "the unique fully-satisfied recipe, or none", add the ambiguous state and its andon light, and — this is the part not to skip — have the machine panel name the recipe it has picked. The moment two recipes can live on one kind, a player needs to be told which one this machine is running, and that is a real UI surface, not a label.

C — Let the player pick

A recipe dropdown on the machine panel. This is what every other factory game does, and it is what the shipped invariant exists specifically to avoid — it turns placement from a spatial puzzle into a configuration chore. Not recommended, and mentioned only so the decision is made on purpose rather than by default.

Recommendation: B, before sauce 01. It is a small change made while there are two sauces, or a large one made while there are eleven.

8 · Deliberately not proposed

  • Ageing. Real mustard rests three days and real hot sauce ferments for weeks, and neither is in the game as a resting mechanic. aged_ketchup and the ageing rack were removed with the note "ageing is not a mechanic this game wants", and nothing here reopens that. The fermenter is not an ageing rack: it is an ordinary machine with a long time_ticks, it occupies the floor while it runs, and its output goes straight down a pipe. House reserve is a prestige tier gated by layout, not by waiting.
  • A spot market. Every sauce here sells through contracts. Nothing in this document needs a place to dump surplus, and adding one would take the teeth out of the contention that most of these sauces are built to create.
  • Spice heat as a stat. Tempting, and wrong: a Scoville number would be a second economy running alongside the first, and none of the fun described above depends on it.
  • Quality tiers. Same argument. A sauce is a sauce; the interesting variable is whether you can make enough of it in time.
  • Per-sauce staff roles. The existing manufacturing crew covers all three new machines, and lined pipe takes no crew at all. A "fermenter tech" role would be a payroll line with no decision attached to it.
